name: Genioplasty

lead: Genioplasty changes chin projection, height or width for a more defined chin and a better-balanced lower face and profile. It is often discussed on looksmax.org as an alternative or complement to double-jaw surgery for a recessed chin.

In a sliding genioplasty a segment of the lower jaw border is cut, moved forward, back or vertically and fixed with a titanium plate; implants add volume instead. The shape change is visible right away once swelling settles. The literature consists mainly of technique papers, accuracy studies of computer-planned surgery and registered trials of fixation and implant methods.

paras: Surgeons include oral and maxillofacial surgeons, plastic surgeons and otolaryngologists. Bone-cut versions are done under general anaesthesia, and people plan the amount of movement with the surgeon using photos and scans.
Reported effects include swelling, temporary or lasting numbness of the lip and chin, infection and implant displacement.

angle.text: Genioplasty moves or reshapes the chin bone, or adds an implant, to improve chin projection and lower-face balance. The shape change is visible once swelling settles, and forum posters discuss it as an alternative to double-jaw surgery.

lead: Genioplasty is chin surgery that changes the projection, height or width of the chin so that it sits in better balance with the nose, lips and jawline in profile. The term covers bone operations, most commonly the sliding genioplasty in which the lower border of the chin bone is cut and repositioned, and it is also used loosely for chin augmentation with implants or fillers.[1][2] Surgeons who perform it include oral and maxillofacial surgeons, plastic surgeons and otolaryngologists.[1]

For appearance, the aim is a more defined lower third of the face: a recessed chin can be brought forward, a long chin shortened, and a wide or short chin reshaped, with the soft tissue of the chin and neck following the bone.[3][2] Reviews describe the chin as a key element of facial harmony and profile balance, and Wikipedia describes bone-based correction as usually giving a larger change than implants.[2][1] It is performed alone, alongside rhinoplasty, or as part of double-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery and facial feminization surgery.[2][4]

In looksmaxxing communities genioplasty is one of the most frequently discussed facial bone procedures: members post profile photos, compare surgeon-quoted advancement figures, weigh it against bimaxillary surgery for a recessed chin, and exchange recovery reports.[5][6][7] The published literature consists of review articles, surgical technique and fixation papers, accuracy studies of computer-planned surgery, nerve-sensation studies and a number of registered trials of implants, plates and recovery aids.[3][8][9][10]
infobox: Facial bone / chin surgery (osteotomy) or implant augmentation

Oral and maxillofacial, plastic and ENT surgeons

Titanium plates and screws, or wires; resorbable and patient-specific plates have been studied

Two oral surgery papers on genioplasty, 1957

paras: Wikipedia groups the main approaches into bone-based and implant-based chin augmentation. Bone manipulation of the mandible usually gives a more dramatic correction than a prosthetic implant, while implants are described as a simpler operation.[1]

In a sliding genioplasty, a horseshoe-shaped piece from the lower border of the chin is cut and moved forward to increase projection, or backward to reduce it, then fixed with a titanium step plate and screws or, in older techniques, with wires and intermaxillary fixation for three to four weeks.[1] The segment can also be moved vertically, so the same operation can lengthen or shorten the chin.[3] Wikipedia's orthognathic surgery article describes the incision as running inside the mouth from the first bicuspid on one side to the first bicuspid on the other, with titanium plates securing the segments and no jaw wiring needed.[11]

The T-osteotomy, also called the mini V-line, was developed by Korean surgeons. It is performed under general anaesthesia from inside the mouth: a horizontal cut leaves a small central bone portion, two vertical cuts remove an inverted trapezoid, and the segments are reattached with pre-bent titanium plates, narrowing the chin and lengthening it by roughly 2 to 3 mm on average.[1] The mentalis muscle, which lifts the lower lip and chin, has to be carefully reattached.[1]

Implants are placed through an incision under the chin or inside the lower lip. Wikipedia lists silicone (soft, smooth and easier to remove, though it can shift or cause bone resorption), porous polyethylene or Medpor (tissue grows into the pores, anchoring it but making removal harder), ePTFE, acellular dermal matrix and other materials, as well as bone grafts taken from the patient's rib or pelvis.[1] Custom implants made from CT-based designs are described as offering a single treatment for unusual anatomy, usually with lower morbidity.[2]

Injectable fillers, mainly hyaluronic acid and calcium hydroxyapatite, are a non-surgical option; results usually last months to years.[1][12] Permanent free silicone injections have fallen out of favour after reports of migration, chronic inflammation and infection.[1]

A review of contemporary orthognathic planning stresses evaluating the chin on its own merit, because its position strongly affects the aesthetics of the lower face and the maxillofacial profile.[3] Wikipedia lists balancing the facial profile, improving the silhouette of the jawline and neck, and self-confidence as reasons patients seek chin augmentation, and notes that a small chin together with a significant overbite may call for orthognathic mandibular advancement, since cosmetic chin procedures alone do not correct the bite.[1]

A 1989 review article from a plastic surgeon described performing 15 chin procedures in 1988, seven osteotomies and eight implants, and noted that only five of 38 rhinoplasty patients (15 per cent) had a simultaneous genioplasty even though the chin matters in nasal surgery; the author called genioplasty a way to improve facial aesthetics with minimal risk and argued for better patient selection.[13]

In facial feminization surgery, chin reshaping is planned with other bone work: Wikipedia notes that male chins tend to be longer, wider and more projecting, and that a sliding genioplasty can reduce chin length, usually combined with jaw reduction.[14][15][4] Retrognathia, a mandible positioned behind its normal location, is the clinical term for the recessed lower face that many forum posters describe.[16]

Two papers published in 1957 in Oral Surgery, Oral Medicine, Oral Pathology described the surgical correction of mandibular prognathism and retrognathia with consideration of genioplasty, covering procedures to reshape the chin and operating methods for microgenia and distoclusion; the first paper has been cited several hundred times.[17][18] In 1958 Aufricht reported combined nose and chin surgery from 27 years of experience.[1] Wikipedia's orthognathic surgery article credits Hugo Obwegeser with popularising the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy and notes that jaw osteotomies date to the 1940s.[11]

Comparisons of bone-based and implant augmentation were published in 1990, and in 2014 Korean surgeons described the T-osteotomy technique for narrowing and lengthening the chin.[1] From the 2010s, computer-aided simulation and patient-specific guides, plates and implants became a research focus.[8][19][20]

A prospective multicentre study of 65 consecutive patients from three centres compared planned with actual outcomes for computer-aided surgical simulation in orthognathic surgery; computer-generated splints were used in all patients, and one centre used computer-generated chin templates to reposition the chin.[8] A later study examined the accuracy of virtual surgical planning in two-jaw surgery.[19]

Registered trials have tested custom-made CAD-CAM titanium miniplates for positioning the chin segment (n=10), a patient-specific PEEK implant for chin deficiency (n=20), patient-specific PEEK versus titanium plates for advancement genioplasty (n=14, completed) and patient-specific implants in genioplasty (n=30).[21][22][23][20] A 2024 randomised trial compared soft-tissue profile changes after autogenous fat grafting or onlay PEEK augmentation with sliding genioplasty for a deficient chin.[24][25] A review describes virtual surgical planning as continuing to offer dependable solutions for small and complex chin position problems.[2]

Wikipedia notes minimal chewing immediately after surgery and soft foods or liquids for a period afterwards.[1] Its orthognathic surgery article gives a general pattern of initial healing over two to six weeks and complete bony healing taking a further two to four months, with return to work after about two to six weeks; those figures describe jaw surgery in general rather than genioplasty alone.[11] Reviews note that the soft tissues around the mandible tend to return toward their original position, which is why secure fixation of the bone segment matters.[2]

Studies of surgical handling have compared incision shapes (18 high labial curvilinear incisions with 27 W-shaped incisions in a randomised trial), resorbable fixation in 20 patients, and piezosurgery for cutting the bone.[26][27][28]

Common effects are swelling, bruising or haematoma, and temporary weakness or numbness of the lower lip; less common ones are infection, bony changes, implant displacement and nerve damage, and Wikipedia states surgeon experience helps reduce complications.[1] The facial feminization article names damage to the mental nerve as the greatest risk, with injury to tooth roots, infection, non-union and mentalis muscle damage also possible.[14] Orthognathic surgery in general carries infection rates of up to 7 per cent in one summary, and facial numbness from nerve damage usually recovers within about three months.[11]

A study of 1,034 orthognathic patients examined after two years assessed light-touch sensation in the mental nerve region after mandibular osteotomies including genioplasty, and found neurosensory deficiency rates that differed by procedure, including 39 per cent after sagittal split ramus osteotomy.[9] Randomised trials have since tested whether leucocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin or concentrated growth factor improve lip sensation after osseous genioplasty.[29][30] Wikipedia notes bone grafts appear linked to higher infection rates, even decades later, and implants can migrate or erode adjacent bone.[1]

Most human research on genioplasty concerns surgical technique, accuracy of planning and recovery, rather than attractiveness outcomes. It includes a prospective multicentre accuracy study (n=65), a neurosensory study of 1,034 orthognathic patients, randomised trials of incision type, resorbable fixation, piezosurgery and healing adjuncts, and a 2024 randomised trial comparing fat or PEEK onlay with sliding genioplasty.[8][9][26][27][28][24]

Registered trials compare box and mini-wing techniques (n=40, started 2019), custom plates and implants, a custom alloplastic implant versus computer-guided genioplasty at one year (n=20), advancement genioplasty with and without submental liposuction (n=22), and electroacupuncture for numbness and swelling after orthognathic surgery and mentoplasty (n=118).[10][21][22][31][32][33] Many are small and several have unknown status. No trial in this literature tests a target number of millimetres of advancement for attractiveness.

Bimaxillary (double-jaw) surgery moves the upper and lower jaws and is used for bite and skeletal discrepancies, with chin repositioning as one planning component.[34][11] Dermal fillers and fat grafting are less invasive ways to alter chin volume.[12][24] Jaw reduction and masseter reduction are used alongside genioplasty in facial feminization.[14][15]

On looksmax.org, members post profile photos asking whether a recessed chin warrants a genioplasty, bimaxillary surgery or neither, and ask others to assess whether the problem lies in the chin, mandible or maxilla.[5] In one thread a poster reported that a surgeon quoted 4 to 5 mm for an average chin, offered more on request, and said the chin could also be lengthened to improve the facial thirds; he asked how many millimetres others thought he needed.[6]

Another thread is titled around the idea that genioplasty is a life-changing surgery, and posts of this kind describe it as a high-impact procedure that can be combined with other facial work.[7] Replies in other threads sometimes tell posters that their profile is not recessed and that the gain would be small, and suggest alternatives such as fat grafting or focusing on other features.[5]

lore.intro: Genioplasty appears on looksmax.org in planning, comparison and recovery threads, frequently framed against bimaxillary surgery.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: Sliding genioplasty can be enough instead of full double-jaw surgery
More millimetres of advancement gives a better chin
A longer chin improves facial thirds
Bone surgery gives a bigger and more lasting change than implants or filler
Genioplasty is a high-impact procedure for a relatively simple operation

timeline.event: Two oral surgery papers describe correction of mandibular prognathism and retrognathia with consideration of genioplasty, including operating methods for microgenia.[17][18]
Aufricht reports combined nose and chin surgery from 27 years of experience.[1]
A Clinics in Plastic Surgery review argues for wider use of genioplasty by osteotomy or implant in aesthetic practice.[13]
Studies compare osteoplastic and alloplastic augmentation genioplasty and biomaterials for facial augmentation.[1]
A randomised trial compares high labial incision shapes for chin osteotomy.[26]
A trial evaluates resorbable fixation devices in genioplasty in 20 patients.[27]
A review describes the state of the art of facial feminization surgery, including chin and jaw procedures.[4]
A prospective multicentre study of 65 patients assesses computer-aided surgical simulation, including chin repositioning.[8]
Korean surgeons describe the T-osteotomy for narrowing and lengthening the chin.[1]
Trials of patient-specific plates and implants for genioplasty begin.[21][22][23][31]
Randomised trials test healing adjuncts after genioplasty and compare fat or PEEK onlay with sliding genioplasty; contemporary reviews are published.[30][29][24][3][2]
